documents: Wege et al. 2022, Earth and Space Science 9, e2021EA002196 (published paper, PDF, 15 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 15, identical to PDF pages counted from 1); supporting information cited as referenced in the main text

entry.evidence: It might be possible to use legacy data to derive shallow seabed properties without the need to conduct field surveys.

steps.action: Propose a processing flow that uses large-offset towed-streamer MCS data and airgun-excited Scholte waves to derive shallow seabed shear-wave velocity.
steps.quote: We report a new strategy on specific data processing flow and combinations of different waveform analysis techniques.

steps.action: Use the 1995 TAICRUST cruise EW9509 line 38 MCS data (160-channel, 4-km streamer, 20-airgun array) across the Taiwan Strait.
steps.quote: The MCS data used in this study were collected in 1995 by the research vessel RV Maurice Ewing (cruise EW9509)

steps.action: Reprocess the line with standard reflection processing and semblance velocity analysis to obtain a depth-migrated section and a P-wave velocity model.
steps.quote: We reprocessed the EW9509-38 seismic transect to derive the P-wave velocity distribution along the profile

steps.action: Compute full-elastic synthetic shot gathers by wavenumber integration for a layered 1D model (Table 1) with streamer-like geometry.
steps.quote: Synthetic full-waveform data were generated by a numerical modeling method called wave-number integration (Herrmann, 2013).

steps.action: Compare shot 900 with the synthetic gather to verify that the low-frequency, low-apparent-velocity phases are Scholte waves.
steps.quote: When using a 1–8 Hz band-pass filter, those waveforms show very high similarity.

steps.action: Set up the phase-shift dispersion imaging, multimode picking, Poisson's-ratio calculation, and the Xia et al. spectral-ratio attenuation and Q estimation.
steps.quote: To transform the shot gathers into the phase velocity-frequency spectrum, we used the phase-shift method (Park et al., 1998).

steps.action: Invert synthetic dispersion picks (three modes, 1-7 Hz) with the Herrmann multimodal inversion and recover the known input Vs model (Figure 4).
steps.quote: We used synthetic waveforms to see if we could successfully recover the 1D shear-wave velocity and attenuation

steps.action: Omit higher modes and high frequencies from the synthetic picks and re-invert to test stability; the fundamental mode up to 3 Hz still resolves the top 150 m.
steps.quote: we systematically omitted higher modes and frequencies of the picked data before inversion

steps.action: Pick fundamental and higher-mode dispersion curves and attenuation factors from 150 field shots at 250 m spacing.
steps.quote: Next, we used the field data to pick the dispersion curves in order to estimate the shear-wave velocity.

steps.action: Invert the 150 dispersion picks into independent 1D Vs models assembled into a pseudo-2D section showing a slow northern zone and a faster southern zone.
steps.quote: Figure 7b displays a pseudo-2D shear-velocity model put together from inversion results of 150 sites along a 37.5 km transect

steps.action: Combine Vp and Vs into dynamic Poisson's ratio (0.45-0.50) and invert attenuation factors for QS, flagging QS as unreliable.
steps.quote: So, we will interpret the inversion results with caution.

steps.action: Run synthetic sensitivity tests varying water depth, receiver depth, source depth, and first-layer Vs to see how the dispersion bandwidth changes.
steps.quote: we have conducted additional sensitivity tests using synthetic waveforms to investigate how variations in the water depth

steps.action: Compute the phase-velocity difference between Scholte and Rayleigh waves for varying water depth to show the water layer must be modelled.
steps.quote: At low frequencies (below 5 Hz), a water depth difference of 10–50 m results in a phase velocity difference of 30–40 m/s

steps.action: Derive recommended acquisition parameters (offsets, group spacing, record length, source and streamer depth) for future Scholte-wave surveys (Table 2).
steps.quote: In Table 2, we show an example of some recommended parameters when studying Scholte waves.

steps.action: Test moving-ship effects with a moveout correction and re-inversion (Figure S12), and compare stacked with unstacked shot gathers.
steps.quote: We then calculated the difference between the original and the corrected S-wave velocity models

steps.action: Interpret the northern low-Vs zone as a loose, fluid-saturated, possibly overpressured ~30 m layer, without excluding a very thin normal layer or sand-wave bathymetry effects.
steps.quote: we propose that there should be a weak or even overpressured layer of about 30 m in shallow depth.

steps.action: Compare the low-velocity interpretation with published sedimentary studies of migrating sand waves on the Changyun Ridge.
steps.quote: [...] low-velocity area is consistent with results from recent sedimentary studies (Liao & Yu, 2005)

steps.action: Check the inverted layering against the independent borehole DA3 gamma-ray log, which shows a lithology change at 30 m.
steps.quote: The gamma ray data of the borehole show lithology change at 30 m sub-bottom depth (Figure 7b) consistent with our inversion result.

steps.action: Retain the claim that legacy large-offset streamer data can yield Vs, Vp, Poisson's ratio and, partly, QS to 150 m, plus the north-south Vs contrast.
steps.quote: This study shows the feasibility of using large-offset streamer data and a strong airgun to excite Scholte waves in shallow marine areas

tree.answer: Airgun-excited Scholte waves recorded on a towed streamer in shallow water
No; Vs is latent and inferred by multimodal dispersion inversion
Characterize the method and estimate Vs and geotechnical properties along the transect
No formal rivals; for the low-Vs zone, a thin normal layer and sand-wave effects are noted but not tested
Field conditions found (legacy survey); synthetic conditions set by the authors
Survives synthetic recovery, mode and frequency omission, moving-system correction, stacking comparison, and qualitative borehole agreement
Kept: capability characterized; Vs model retained, QS with low confidence

end.claim: Large-offset towed-streamer MCS data with a strong airgun can excite Scholte waves in water shallower than 50 m and be inverted for Vs, Vp, Poisson's ratio and, to an extent, QS down to 150 m sub-bottom depth.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the multimodal inversion of field Scholte-wave dispersion picks into the pseudo-2D Vs section, there would be no demonstration that streamer data yield seabed Vs.

gates.evidence: Legacy 1995 data were collected for crustal geodynamics, not for this hypothesis. The method could have failed the synthetic recovery test (Figure 4, p. 6) and the comparison with synthetic waveforms (p. 4). Field Vs is checked only qualitatively against one borehole (p. 13). No analysis, threshold, or hypothesis is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW) and Poisson's ratio as a geotechnical parameter
Fast 1D Fourier transform for decomposing traces into frequency components

novelty_claims.quote: However, to the best of our knowledge, to date, there have been no systematic synthetic waveform tests on streamer data.
We report a new strategy on specific data processing flow and combinations of different waveform analysis techniques.
This new approach can help to investigate the seabed geotechnical properties of shallow water areas.

limits: No peer-review file was supplied; the acknowledgments mention anonymous reviewers, but no review sequence can be coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: (1) the pseudo-2D Vs model is estimate_with_resolution, with error bounded only by synthetic tests (5%-10%, Figure S5) and no per-site uncertainty; (2) QS is reported with low confidence and implausible values (<0, >300) are attributed to noise, so it is at most a weak estimate; (3) the weak or overpressured 30 m layer in the north is a best_explanation that is not tested against the thin-layer or sand-wave alternatives the authors themselves mention. The borehole check is a single, qualitative visual comparison. The inversion assumes a flat seafloor and fixed layer thicknesses. Inference: the picking of modes per shot was done by hand, and the criteria for picking or rejecting shots are not documented. The initial model is partly tuned to the data (an initial inversion), so the agreement in Figure 3 is not fully independent of the field data. The sensitivity tests use one base model, so generalization to other seabeds is untested with field data.

disagreements.target: Ritzwoller and Levshin (2002), on the ideal source position for marine multicomponent data
disagreements.support: Synthetic receiver-depth tests (Figure 9) show a wider dispersion bandwidth as the streamer approaches the seafloor, adding to the source-depth recommendation.
disagreements.quote: However, we add that it is also advantageous if the streamer is lowered to receive a broader band signal.

disagreements.target: Zhang and Chan (2003), on inversion accuracy depending mostly on low-frequency phase velocities
disagreements.support: The authors' frequency-omission tests suggest the low-frequency part can be a pitfall when higher frequencies are missing; they set this against Zhang and Chan's statement.
disagreements.quote: On the other hand, Zhang and Chan (2003) stated that the accuracy of the inversion is mostly sensitive to phase velocities at lower frequencies.

disagreements.target: Mode-free inversion approaches (Ernst, 2008; Maraschini et al., 2010)
disagreements.support: Citing Foti et al. (2002), the authors argue that a large enough receiver array separates modes well, so explicit mode picking is justified.
disagreements.quote: However, if the receiver array is large enough (number of receivers and offset) modes separate very well in the dispersion image

disagreements.target: The spatial-aliasing limit set by streamer channel spacing (cf. Klein et al., 2005)
disagreements.support: In their field case, signals beyond the theoretical aliasing boundary showed little aliasing.
disagreements.quote: However, we found in our case study that signals beyond the boundary of spatial aliasing had little to no spatially aliased signals.

disagreements.target: Common practice of stacking marine shot gathers to improve signal-to-noise ratio
disagreements.support: Comparing inversions of stacked and unstacked gathers, they found stacking can harm Scholte arrivals and reduce lateral resolution.
disagreements.quote: we found that stacking would sometimes cause more harm to the arrivals of the Scholte waves than it would increase the signal-to-noise ratio.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Top and bottom muting around the fundamental-mode wave train
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Mode separation with a High-Resolution Linear Radon Transform (Luo et al., 2008)

alternatives_considered.reason: Stacking can stack incoherent phases on an irregular seafloor and lowers resolution over 250 m

alternatives_considered.chosen: Uncorrected shot gathers from the moving streamer
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Moveout correction with a constant 200 m/s S-wave velocity
alternatives_considered.reason: The difference in inverted Vs is small

alternatives_considered.chosen: Explicit mode picking for multimodal inversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Inversion without mode identification (Ernst, 2008; Maraschini et al., 2010)
alternatives_considered.reason: Modes separate well with a large receiver array

alternatives_considered.chosen: Theoretical dispersion curves that include the water layer
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Rayleigh-wave dispersion without the water layer
alternatives_considered.reason: Water depth changes phase velocity by 30-40 m/s below 5 Hz
